correctness.rationale: The exhaustive domain decomposition into r^2st, 4pq, 2p^2q and 2pq^2 is sound for omega=3, Omega=4. The odd inequality sigma(n)/n <= 624/315 < 2 eliminates all odd cases. For 4pq, Delta=(7-p)q+7(p+1) eliminates p>=13 and bounds q<=7(p+1) for p=3,5,7; p=11 has q<21. For 2p^2q, Delta=(3+3p-p^2)q+3(p^2+p+1) eliminates p>=7, with exact candidate reduction p=3: q in {5,7,11}; p=5: q in {7,11,13}. For 2pq^2, Delta=(3-p)q^2+3(p+1)(q+1) eliminates p>=7 and reduces p=5 to q=7, p=3 to q in {5,7,11}. The actual independent checker reconstructs all divisor sets and every unordered omitted pair for the resulting 32+6+4 finite candidates; it finds the specified ten numbers and precisely one pair for each. The infinite conclusion rests on the algebraic exclusion and not on a finite extrapolation. The exact script and proof are embedded.

originality.rationale: The full omega(n)=3, Omega(n)=4 classification is not implied by a classification at two-prime support, by the published squarefree 2pq classification (Omega=3), by the previously obtained 2p^2q subclass, or by numerical tables of initial 2-near-perfect examples. The 2025/2026 primary paper explicitly names three-prime-support families as future work. All available close records were compared by implication, not title alone.

value.rationale: The exact first nonsquarefree three-prime-support layer is a natural and complete classification indexed by omega(n)=3 and Omega(n)=4. It answers a precisely motivated part of the published three-support classification program, not an arbitrary numeric slice: three distinct primes require Omega>=3, so Omega=4 is the immediately next exponent layer. It determines all ten values and all unique omitted-divisor pairs, proves the absence of odd and 2pq^2 examples, and supplies explicit finite algebraic cutoffs. The 2025/2026 primary source identifies three-prime-support 2-near-perfect families as a future classification problem. The four previously covered 2p^2q cases do not imply the remaining six 4pq cases or exclusions. No universal larger-support conjecture is claimed.
